title: Why Making Money In An MLM Is Impossible
summary: Simple layered model showing an MLM pay structure leaves the bottom eighty percent ineligible to earn and the next tiers in the red after fees and events.

assertions.quote: becoming successful in an mlm is mathematically impossible regardless of your level of effort or your mindset
you can see how quickly and easily these costs are gonna eat up the money that we're making from the compensation plan

verdicts.note: The report documents membership fees, required or encouraged product purchases to keep rank or 'active' status, website, advertising, training and conference costs, with court findings and participant comments of buying hundreds of dollars of product monthly; expenses can and in some MLMs often do exceed income.

All MLM ventures required upfront spending on inventory, marketing materials and training; but two-thirds of participants spent under $1,000 in total, 24% spent $1,000-$4,999 and 11% $5,000 or more, so the drain is real but usually modest.
Income disclosures ignore participant expenses even though expenses can, and in some MLMs often do, outstrip income.

Beyond sign-up, Taylor found $50-$500 a month in incentivised product purchases needed to qualify for commissions, plus training, conferences, books, recordings and sales 'tools' that upline promoters expect downline participants to buy.

assertions.quote: that can only happen 13 times before you run out of people on earth to recruit

verdicts.note: In nearly every rank-based disclosure the vast majority of participants sit in the two or three lowest ranks (one example: 92.37% in the bottom rank averaging $41.69, top ranks fractions of a percent), confirming most are structurally at the bottom; the report does not test the exponential-exhaustion arithmetic.

Among former participants, 29% left because the commission structure mostly benefited those at the top and 25% because the market was saturated with other sellers; self-reported reasons, not a structural test.

Taylor says recruitment inevitably dries up as the market saturates and the vast majority of participants are then guaranteed to be at the bottom; he illustrates with an 8-ball pyramid reaching 8,191 people in 10 cycles but does not do the population-exhaustion arithmetic.

assertions.quote: they also call themselves network marketing peer-to-peer marketing direct sales

verdicts.note: The terms are used interchangeably by MLMs, though some direct-sales models pay no recruitment-based commissions.

AARP defines MLM, or network marketing, as a type of direct selling in which members earn from their own sales and from their direct and indirect recruits' sales, confirming the labels describe one downline model; it treats pyramid schemes as a distinct, illegal subset rather than equating them.

Taylor treats MLM as a pyramid scheme but explicitly distinguishes it from other direct-sales programs that pay the seller 20-50% commission and focus on end customers, so not all direct selling is the same pyramid.

assertions.quote: paying for the tickets of your downline is a great way of holding something over their head in the future

verdicts.note: Consistent with ex-member accounts and high-control-group literature but not systematically measured.
